summary_grc: ἀνὴρ ἀδύνατος ἐν τῇ βουλῇ ἀπολογεῖται· ὁ γὰρ κατήγορός φησιν αὐτὸν οὐ δικαίως τὸ ἀργύριον λαμβάνειν.
summary_en: Athens paid disabled citizens with no other income an obol a day, and the Council checked the list each year. An accuser says one of them can ride horses and earn a living. His answer, written by Lysias, lightly cut: an old craftsman, no inheritance, no children, and a trade that no longer feeds him.
caption_grc: πρόσοδος δέ μοι οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλη πλὴν ταύτης.

original.note: Lysias 24, For the Disabled Man, sections 4–6, lightly cut; the speech was written in the early fourth century (after 403 BC) for a man to deliver himself before the Council (ὦ βουλή). The first sentences of 24.4 and all of 24.5 after the first two proofs are left out. The Perseus text prints οἴμαι for οἶμαι.

sentences.text: ἡ πόλις τῶν Ἀθηναίων τοῖς ἀδυνάτοις, οἳ διὰ συμφορὰν τοῦ σώματος ἐργάζεσθαι οὐ δύνανται, ὀβολὸν τῆς ἡμέρας δίδωσιν.
ἑκάστου δὲ ἔτους ἡ βουλὴ τοὺς ἀδυνάτους δοκιμάζει, καὶ ἔξεστι τῷ βουλομένῳ κατηγορεῖν.
ποτὲ δὲ κατήγορός τις, ὡς λέγουσιν, διὰ φθόνον ἀνδρὶ χωλῷ ἐπεβούλευσεν, ὃς ἵπποις ἐχρῆτο διὰ τὸ ἀσθενὲς σῶμα.
ὁ δὲ ἀνήρ, ἡγούμενος τὸν κατήγορον ψεύδεσθαι, λόγον παρὰ τοῦ Λυσίου ἔλαβεν καὶ ἐν τῇ βουλῇ οὕτως εἶπεν·

glosses.value: Lysias wrote speeches for others to deliver (he was a λογογράφος); the speaker learned it by heart

glosses.value: φησί + accusative and infinitive: 'he says that I …' (indirect statement)

glosses.value: still reported speech: (he says that I) am able in body and am not one of the disabled

to help, to be of use (ὠφελέω)

notice: φησὶ γὰρ ὁ κατήγορος οὐ δικαίως με λαμβάνειν τὸ παρὰ τῆς πόλεως ἀργύριον
τῆς μὲν τοῦ σώματος ῥώμης … τῆς δ’ ἐν τῇ τέχνῃ εὐπορίας
τὴν δὲ μητέρα τελευτήσασαν πέπαυμαι τρέφων
παῖδες δέ μοι οὔπω εἰσὶν οἵ με θεραπεύσουσι
ἣν ἂν ἀφέλησθέ με, κινδυνεύσαιμ’ ἂν …

grammar.md:
**Reading Lysias: the plain style.** Lysias wrote for ordinary Athenians, and he made them sound ordinary: short words, clear order, no showing off. But each sentence is carefully built. Watch for three things.

**1. The charge in reported speech.** A defendant first states the accusation, in the accusative and infinitive after φησί: φησὶ γὰρ ὁ κατήγορος οὐ δικαίως **με λαμβάνειν** … καὶ … **δύνασθαι** καὶ οὐκ **εἶναι** … καὶ … **ἐπίστασθαι**. Every infinitive hangs on the one φησί, even across a full stop in our text. Then he answers in the first person indicative: ἐμοὶ γὰρ ὁ μὲν πατὴρ κατέλιπεν οὐδέν …

**2. μέν … δέ in balance.** τῆς **μὲν** τοῦ σώματος ῥώμης …, τῆς **δ’** ἐν τῇ τέχνῃ εὐπορίας; ὁ **μὲν** πατὴρ …, τὴν **δὲ** μητέρα …, παῖδες **δὲ** …; ἣν αὐτὸς **μὲν** …, τὸν διαδεξόμενον **δ’** …. Lysias lays out his life in pairs so that the Council can follow without effort.

**3. The softened threat.** ἣν ἂν ἀφέλησθέ με, κινδυνεύσαιμ’ ἂν … 'which (income) if you take from me, I would risk …'. A relative + ἄν + subjunctive stands for ἐάν (future more vivid); the main verb is a **potential optative** with ἄν (Unit 10), more modest than the future κινδυνεύσω.

**Also:** the **dative of possession** (παῖδες δέ μοι οὔπω εἰσίν 'I have no children yet'; πρόσοδος δέ μοι οὐκ ἔστιν 'I have no income'); παύομαι + participle 'stop doing'; a relative with the future indicative for purpose (οἵ με θεραπεύσουσι 'who will look after me'); crasis κἀγώ = καὶ ἐγώ.

culture.title: Welfare in Athens
culture.md:
Athens had no hospitals and no pensions in our sense, but it did support some citizens who could not support themselves. War orphans were brought up at public expense until they came of age and then presented with a hoplite's armour in the theatre. And, as Aristotle records (*Constitution of the Athenians* 49.4), a citizen who owned less than three minas and was disabled in body so that he could not work was entitled to a public allowance, one obol a day in Lysias' time and two in Aristotle's. Each year the **Council** examined the list (δοκιμασία), and any citizen could object that a man did not qualify.

That is the setting of Lysias 24. The speaker is a craftsman, lame, who rides borrowed horses because he cannot walk far, and who has a small shop where men meet and talk. The accuser, he says, is acting from envy. Most of the speech is comic: he pretends that if he is fit enough to lose his obol, he is fit enough to be chosen by lot as one of the nine archons. Whether he won, we do not know. The speech is our best evidence for the life of a poor disabled man in classical Athens (the picture shows an Athenian grave relief of a man leaning on his staff), and it was written by the most admired speechwriter of the day, himself a metic who had lost almost everything under the Thirty.
